key_terms.meaning: A self-generating sensor that converts the measurand directly into electrical energy, such as a thermocouple or piezoelectric sensor.
A sensor that needs an external supply and changes its resistance, capacitance or inductance when the measurand changes.
The physical quantity being measured, such as temperature, pressure or strain.
A device that converts an electrical signal back into a physical quantity, such as a loudspeaker or actuator.
Change of a material's resistance when it is mechanically strained; used in strain gauges and pressure sensors.
Production of an emf in a circuit of two dissimilar metals whose junctions are at different temperatures; the basis of a thermocouple.
The documented comparison of a sensor's output with a reference standard of known uncertainty.
An unbroken chain of calibrations, each with stated uncertainty, linking the sensor to a national or international standard.
The rungs of the calibration ladder below the SI definitions, each calibrated against the one above.
How close the mean reading is to the true value; quoted as ± value, ± %FS or ± % of reading.
How closely repeated readings agree with one another under the same conditions; also called repeatability.
The smallest change of input that produces a detectable change in output.
The change of output divided by the change of input, S = Δy/Δx.
How closely the sensor's calibration curve follows a straight line over its range.
The difference in output for the same input when approached from increasing and decreasing directions.
For a first-order sensor, the time to reach 63.2 % of the final output after a step; τ = mc/(hA) for a thermocouple bead.
For a second-order sensor, the ratio of actual damping to critical damping; it sets overshoot and ringing.
The undamped frequency at which a second-order sensor would oscillate freely.
A repeatable error that shifts all readings in the same direction, also called bias.
A scatter in repeated readings that varies unpredictably; reduced by averaging.
A parameter that characterises the range of values within which the true value is expected to lie.

takeaways: Active sensors generate their own electrical signal; passive sensors need an external excitation supply and modify it.
Every sensor rests on a physical law that converts the measurand into a change of resistance, capacitance, inductance or emf.
Calibration is a documented comparison against a traceable standard, not just an adjustment of the zero knob.
Static characteristics answer different questions: accuracy is closeness to truth, precision is repeatability, and resolution is the smallest detectable change.
Linearity, hysteresis and drift describe how far a real sensor departs from an ideal straight-line response.
First-order sensors lag with a time constant τ; second-order sensors add overshoot and ringing set by damping ratio ζ and natural frequency ωₙ.
Error analysis separates systematic bias from random scatter and reports a best estimate with an uncertainty.
A measurement chain from sensor to display must be analysed as a system, because each block adds its own error and lag.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine the classification of transducers, static and dynamic characteristics and error analysis, with a worked numerical example; most syllabi also ask for the hierarchy of standards and the calibration procedure.

bank.q: Compare active and passive sensors. Explain how the classification decides wiring and signal conditioning, and give two examples of each.
outline: Define active and passive sensors with self-generating and externally energised behaviour.
Examples: thermocouple and piezoelectric sensor as active; strain gauge and thermistor as passive.
Active sensors need no excitation but may need high-impedance amplifiers.
Passive sensors need a stable supply and a bridge or divider circuit.
Mention output form and typical signal-conditioning blocks.
answer: Definitions. An active (self-generating) sensor converts energy taken from the measurand directly into an electrical output; it needs no supply to sense. A passive (externally energised) sensor changes one of its electrical parameters, resistance, inductance or capacitance, when the measurand changes, and an external supply turns that change into a voltage or current.

The deciding question. Ask where the energy in the output signal comes from. From the measurand: active. From a battery or excitation source: passive. A sensor whose amplifier needs a supply is not active for that reason; the label describes the sensing element only.

Examples. Active: a thermocouple (Seebeck emf, about 41 µV/°C for type K), a piezoelectric crystal (charge q = d·F under force), a photovoltaic cell and a tachogenerator. Passive: an RTD such as Pt100, a thermistor, a strain gauge, a potentiometer, an LVDT and a capacitive sensor. In a hospital, the crystal of an ultrasound probe receiving echoes is active; the thermistor of a temperature probe is passive.

answer.text: Wiring of an active sensor. The sensor is a source with an emf e and a source resistance Rs. The amplifier input Rin forms a divider with it, so the voltage read is e·Rin/(Rin + Rs). With e = 25 mV and Rs = 500 Ω:

answer: So the signal conditioning for an active sensor is a high-input-impedance amplifier (an instrumentation amplifier or a charge amplifier for a piezoelectric crystal), plus what the principle needs: cold-junction compensation for a thermocouple, a charge amplifier that sets the low-frequency limit for a piezo element.

Wiring of a passive sensor. The sensor needs excitation: a constant current, or a voltage feeding a divider or a Wheatstone bridge. The signal is ΔV = I × ΔR for a current-excited resistor. A Pt100 at 100.0 Ω run at 1 mA gives 100 mV and dissipates P = I²R = (10⁻³)² × 100 = 0.10 mW, which warms the element: the excitation level is part of the measurement design.

Signal conditioning for a passive sensor: a stable excitation source (its drift appears directly in the output, unless the circuit is ratiometric), a bridge to null the large standing output, a differential amplifier, and for inductive or capacitive sensors an AC carrier with a demodulator.

Check. A photodiode shows the rule is about the operating mode, not the device: with zero bias, light generates the emf (active); with 5 V reverse bias, light only changes the current the supply drives (passive).

bank.q: State four physical principles used in sensors. Explain how each converts a measurand into an electrical quantity.
outline: Variable resistance: strain gauge, thermistor.
Variable capacitance: parallel-plate capacitive pressure sensor.
Variable inductance: LVDT or reluctance sensor.
Thermoelectric emf: thermocouple.
Piezoelectric charge: piezoelectric accelerometer.
For each, name the physical law and the electrical output.
answer: Idea. Every sensor uses a physical law that converts the non-electrical measurand into a change of an electrical quantity: resistance, capacitance, inductance, emf or charge. Name the law, the measurand, the intermediate change and the output for each principle.

1. Variable resistance (strain and temperature). R = ρL/A. Stretching a wire raises L and lowers A; the strain-gauge equation is ΔR/R = GF·ε with GF ≈ 2 for metal foil. A 120 Ω gauge with GF = 2 at a strain of 500 × 10⁻⁶ changes by 120 × 2 × 500 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.12 Ω. Thermistors and RTDs use the change of ρ with temperature. Output: ΔR, read in a bridge. Use: load cells, the disposable blood-pressure transducer.

2. Variable capacitance. C = ε₀εrA/d. Pressure moves a diaphragm and changes d; humidity changes εr; a moving plate changes A. With A = 25 mm² and d = 0.10 mm of air, C = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 25 × 10⁻⁶/10⁻⁴ = 2.21 pF; closing the gap to 0.09 mm gives 2.46 pF, an 11.1 % rise for a 10 % gap change, so the response is non-linear in d. Output: ΔC, read with an AC bridge or charge amplifier.

3. Variable inductance and induction. L ≈ N²µA/l. A moving iron core changes the reluctance of the magnetic path and so the inductance; in an LVDT it changes the coupling between a primary and two secondaries. Faraday’s law e = −N·dΦ/dt gives an emf when flux changes, the basis of tachogenerators and the electromagnetic blood-flow meter. Output: ΔL (with an AC carrier) or emf.

4. Thermoelectric emf. Two dissimilar metals joined at two junctions at different temperatures give an emf e = S·ΔT (Seebeck effect). With S = 40 µV/°C and ΔT = 25 °C, e = 1.0 mV. The output depends on the temperature difference, so the reference junction must be known or compensated. Output: a small DC emf, read by a high-impedance amplifier.

5. Piezoelectric charge. A force on quartz or PZT displaces charge: q = d·F. With d = 2.3 pC/N (quartz) and F = 10 N, q = 23 pC. The charge leaks away, so the sensor reads changing forces only: vibration, impact, ultrasound echoes. Output: charge, converted by a charge amplifier.

Check. Resistive, capacitive and inductive sensors are passive (they need excitation); thermoelectric and piezoelectric ones are active. The same law can serve two measurands; the packaging decides which one the outside world can change.

bank.q: Explain calibration, verification, adjustment and traceability. Why is traceability necessary in a calibration record?
outline: Calibration: comparison with a standard and recording results.
Verification: checking that the instrument meets a specification.
Adjustment: physical change to bring output closer to the true value.
Traceability: unbroken chain of comparisons with stated uncertainties to a national standard.
Traceability makes readings legally and technically defensible.
answer: Calibration. The documented comparison of an instrument’s output with known inputs produced by a standard of smaller uncertainty, under stated conditions. It is a measurement and a record; it need not change the instrument. Its result is a table or line of deviations with their uncertainty, written on a certificate.

Verification. A pass/fail check that the instrument’s error lies within stated limits, for example ±0.5 %FS. A verified instrument has not necessarily been calibrated: verification gives a verdict, calibration gives the numbers.

Adjustment. The physical or software change of zero and span so that the output matches the ideal line. The order is: calibrate (“as found”), adjust zero then span, recheck zero because the two interact, then calibrate again (“as left”).

answer.text: Worked illustration. A 0–200 kPa sensor checked against a dead-weight tester at 25 °C and 10 V supply gave:

answer: Sensitivity = 3.98 V/200 kPa = 19.9 mV/kPa; zero 0.02 V; largest deviation from the end-point line 0.030 V at 100 kPa = 0.75 % of the 3.98 V span; hysteresis 0.04 V = 1.0 %FS. That is the calibration. If the tolerance is ±1 %FS, verification passes on linearity and is borderline on hysteresis. Adjustment would remove the 0.02 V zero offset but cannot remove hysteresis.

Traceability. An unbroken chain of calibrations, each with a stated uncertainty and documented, linking the result to the SI units through national primary standards. A typical chain: SI definition (fixed constants since 2019) → national primary standard at the national metrology institute → secondary standard of an accredited calibration laboratory → working standard (the dead-weight tester) → the field sensor. Each rung is four to ten times more accurate than the one below.

Why traceability is necessary in a calibration record. (i) It makes the stated uncertainty meaningful, because each link’s uncertainty is known and can be combined. (ii) It makes results from two laboratories, or two hospitals, comparable. (iii) It is demanded by quality systems and regulators: an auditor asks for the certificate of the standard used, and of the standard that calibrated it. (iv) It dates the claim: when a certificate expires the chain is broken, and accuracy can no longer be claimed even if the readings repeat well.

Check. Traceability does not make an instrument accurate; it makes its error known. A sensor with a 2 % error and a valid traceable certificate is usable with a correction; a sensor that repeats to 0.1 % with no certificate has unknown accuracy.

bank.q: Define accuracy, precision, resolution, sensitivity, linearity, span, range and dead band. Give one practical example of each.
outline: Accuracy versus precision with a target analogy.
Resolution as smallest detectable input change.
Sensitivity as Δy/Δx with units.
Linearity as maximum deviation from a best-fit or end-point straight line.
Range = the input limits; span = their difference.
Dead band as input change that produces no output change.
answer: Take one example sensor throughout: a pressure sensor, range 0–250 kPa, output 0–50 mV.

Range. The input limits the sensor is made for: 0 to 250 kPa. Span. The difference of the limits: 250 − 0 = 250 kPa. A 50–250 kPa sensor has the same upper limit but a span of 200 kPa, so range and span are different ideas.

Sensitivity. The slope of output against input, S = Δy/Δx. Here S = 50 mV/250 kPa = 0.2 mV/kPa. A disposable blood-pressure transducer is rated 5 µV/V/mmHg: at 5 V excitation it gives 25 µV/mmHg, so 120 mmHg gives 3.0 mV.

Accuracy. How close the mean reading is to the true value, quoted as ± value, ± %FS or ± % of reading. Ten readings at a true 100 kPa with mean 99.6 kPa have a bias of −0.4 kPa = −0.16 %FS. ±1 %FS allows ±2.5 kPa at any reading; ±1 % of reading allows only ±0.1 kPa at 10 kPa.

Precision. How closely repeated readings agree, as a standard deviation or a band. With s = 0.5 kPa, the 3s band is ±1.5 kPa = ±0.6 %FS. A precise instrument can be inaccurate: a fixed bias moves the mean while the readings stay close together (a tight cluster of shots away from the bull’s-eye).
Resolution. The smallest input change that gives a detectable output change. A display reading 100.1 kPa resolves 0.1 kPa = 0.04 %FS. A clinical thermometer resolving 0.1 °C is an everyday example.

Linearity. The largest deviation of the calibration curve from a stated straight line (end-point, best-fit or independent), as %FS. A curve that bows 0.6 mV above the end-point line has non-linearity 0.6/0.2 = 3 kPa = 1.2 %FS.

Dead band. The input range over which the output does not change at all, typically when the input reverses direction, caused by backlash or friction. A dial gauge whose pointer does not move until the input has reversed by 0.5 kPa has a 0.5 kPa dead band. (Threshold is the smallest input that moves the output from rest at zero.)

Check. Every %FS figure divides by the 250 kPa span: 0.4/250 = 0.16 %, 1.5/250 = 0.6 %, 3/250 = 1.2 %. The largest static error here is linearity, thirty times the resolution, so a finer display would not improve this sensor.

bank.q: Distinguish systematic, random and gross errors. Define absolute error, relative error and percentage error.
outline: Systematic error or bias: repeatable shift, correctable by calibration.
Random error: scatter, reduced by averaging and statistics.
Gross error or blunder: human mistake, rejected, not averaged.
Absolute error = measured − true, with units.
Relative error = absolute error / true value.
Percentage error = relative error × 100%.
answer: Gross errors (blunders). Human or procedural mistakes: reading the wrong scale, writing 1.98 as 1.89, using the wrong range or unit, a loose lead. They are large and irregular. Statistics cannot correct them; they are prevented by care and checks, and found by repeating the measurement. A reading many standard deviations from the rest is a candidate, rejected only with a stated rule and a recorded cause.

Systematic errors (bias). Errors with the same sign and nearly the same size on every repeat. Sources: instrumental (calibration offset, scale-factor error, zero drift), environmental (temperature, supply voltage, magnetic fields), loading (a meter drawing current from the circuit it measures), and method (a blood-pressure cuff too small for the arm reads high every time). Averaging does not reduce them; they are found by calibration against a standard and removed by a correction.

Random errors. Small unpredictable variations from noise, vibration, supply ripple and thermal agitation. They change sign and size from reading to reading. They are described by the standard deviation s of repeated readings, and the mean of n independent readings has standard uncertainty s/√n, so averaging reduces them.
Absolute error. e = xm − xtrue, in the unit of the reading, where xm is the measured value and xtrue the true (accepted) value. The correction is −e.
Relative error. er = (xm − xtrue)/xtrue, dimensionless. Percentage error = er × 100 %.

answer.text: Worked example. A voltmeter reads 5.10 V across a 5.00 V reference.

answer: How averaging separates them. Ten readings of a 5.000 V reference with mean 5.000 V and s = 18.3 mV have zero bias and a standard uncertainty of the mean 18.3/√10 = 5.8 mV. If the meter also had a +0.2 V calibration offset, the mean of ten, or of a thousand, readings would still be 0.2 V high: only the 5.8 mV term shrinks with n.

Reducing each kind. Gross errors: two people read critical values, ranges are checked before reading, and an automatic data logger replaces hand copying. Systematic errors: calibrate against a traceable standard, apply the correction, hold or compensate the influencing inputs (temperature, supply), and choose a meter whose input impedance makes loading negligible. Random errors: shield and ground the leads, filter the signal, and average n readings so that the scatter of the mean falls as 1/√n.
Check. Classify each error by asking: is it a mistake (gross), does it repeat (systematic), or does it scatter (random)? Then the cure follows: repeat, calibrate, or average.

bank.q: A passive sensor has resistance 500 Ω at 0 kPa and 520 Ω at 100 kPa. It is connected in a voltage divider with a 500 Ω series resistor and a 5 V supply. Calculate the output at 0 kPa and at 100 kPa, and the sensitivity in mV/kPa.
outline: Use Vout = 5 × R / (R + 500).
At 0 kPa: Vout = 2.500 V.
Change = 0.049 V = 49 mV.
Sensitivity = 49 mV / 100 kPa = 0.49 mV/kPa.
State that the response is nonlinear and sensitivity is an average over the range.
answer: Circuit. The sensor R is the lower arm of a divider with a fixed 500 Ω resistor on top, fed from 5 V; the output is taken across the sensor: Vout = 5 × R/(R + 500).
Average sensitivity. S = 49.0 mV/100 kPa = 0.490 mV/kPa. In terms of the sensor: the resistance sensitivity is 20 Ω/100 kPa = 0.2 Ω/kPa, and the circuit converts it at 49.0/20 = 2.45 mV/Ω.

answer.text: Linearity check at mid-range, 50 kPa, if the sensor itself is linear (R = 510 Ω):

answer: The divider curve sits 0.24 mV above the end-point line at mid-range, 0.24/49.0 = 0.5 % of the output change. The response is non-linear because R appears in both the numerator and the denominator; the sensitivity quoted is an average over the range.

Practical points. (i) The 2.500 V standing output is fifty times the 49 mV signal; a bridge, with a second divider of two 500 Ω resistors as reference, removes it and lets a differential amplifier use full gain. (ii) The output is proportional to the 5 V supply: a 1 % supply drift is a 25 mV error at zero, half the full signal, unless the reading is ratiometric. (iii) The sensor carries 5/1000 = 5 mA and dissipates (5 × 10⁻³)² × 500 = 12.5 mW, which may heat it.

Better circuit, worked. In a quarter bridge, the reference half gives exactly 2.500 V, so the differential output is 0 V at 0 kPa and 49.0 mV at 100 kPa; an amplifier of gain 50 then gives 2.45 V full scale. The divider’s own sensitivity is greatest when the fixed resistor equals the sensor resistance (here 500 Ω), which is why the 500 Ω value was a good choice: with 1 kΩ on top the output would change by only 5 × 520/1520 − 5 × 500/1500 = 43.9 mV.
Check. The current at 100 kPa is 5/1020 = 4.902 mA; 4.902 mA × 520 Ω = 2.549 V, the same output.

bank.q: A 0–10 bar pressure transmitter gives these outputs. Increasing: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 bar give 0.00, 0.98, 1.97, 3.01, 4.02, 5.00 V. Decreasing: 0.04, 1.06, 2.07, 3.09, 4.07, 5.00 V. Find the output span, the average sensitivity, the hysteresis and the maximum non-linearity (end-point line), each as %FS, and draw the calibration curve.
outline: Output span = full-scale output − zero output
Average sensitivity = output span ÷ input span
Hysteresis = largest decreasing − increasing difference at one input
Non-linearity from the end-point line, on the mean curve
Express each in volts, bar and %FS
Labelled calibration curve
answer: Output span. Increasing readings run from 0.00 V at 0 bar to 5.00 V at 10 bar, so the output span is 5.00 − 0.00 = 5.00 V; the input span is 10 bar.
Average sensitivity. S = 5.00 V/10 bar = 0.500 V/bar. End-point line: Vline = 0.500 × P.

Hysteresis. The largest down − up difference is 0.10 V at 4 bar. As %FS: 0.10/5.00 × 100 = 2.0 %FS; in pressure, 0.10/0.500 = 0.20 bar. Note that the decreasing curve does not return to zero: 0.04 V at 0 bar, a sign of friction or creep in the element.

Non-linearity. Hysteresis is quoted separately, so linearity is judged on the mean of the two curves. The largest |mean − line| is 0.050 V at 6 bar: 0.050/5.00 × 100 = 1.0 %FS (0.10 bar). For the increasing curve alone the largest deviation is 0.03 V at 4 bar, 0.6 %FS; for the decreasing curve alone, 0.09 V at 6 bar, 1.8 %FS. Always say which curve and which straight line.

answer.text: Calibration curve. Output against pressure: the end-point line from (0, 0) to (10, 5.00), the increasing points just under it in the middle, the decreasing points above it, the 0.10 V gap at 4 bar marked as hysteresis.

answer: Method in general. Take readings at five to ten points, first rising then falling, without overshooting a point and coming back. Hold temperature and supply constant and record them. Hysteresis comes from the two branches; linearity from the mean curve against the chosen line; the line must be named on the certificate (end-point here; a least-squares line usually gives a smaller figure for the same data).
Check. Mean at 6 bar = (3.01 + 3.09)/2 = 3.05 V; 3.05 − 3.00 = 0.05 V. Hysteresis is twice the non-linearity, so friction, not the shape of the element, is this transmitter’s main static fault.

bank.q: A first-order temperature sensor has a time constant of 2 s. It is suddenly placed in a bath whose temperature steps by 40 °C. Find the output at 2 s, the time to reach 95% of the step, and the reading error at 10 s.
outline: First-order step response: y(t) = A(1 − e<sup>−t/τ</sup>).
At t = τ = 2 s, output reaches 63.2% of 40 °C = 25.3 °C.
For 95%, t = 3τ = 6 s.
At 10 s, fraction = 1 − e<sup>−5</sup> = 0.9933.
Reading error = 40 × e<sup>−5</sup> = 0.27 °C.
State assumptions: single time constant, no self-heating.
answer: Model. A first-order sensor obeys τ dy/dt + y = Kx. For a step of size A from rest, y(t) = A(1 − e−t/τ) (taking K = 1 °C per °C). Here A = 40 °C and τ = 2 s.
Output at 2 s. t/τ = 1: y = 40(1 − e−1) = 40 × 0.6321 = 25.28 °C. At one time constant the sensor has covered 63.2 % of the step.
Time to 95 %. 1 − e−t/τ = 0.95, so e−t/τ = 0.05 and t = −τ ln 0.05 = 2 × 2.996 = 5.99 s, that is about 3τ = 6 s.
Error at 10 s. t/τ = 5: y = 40(1 − e−5) = 40 × 0.99326 = 39.73 °C. The dynamic error is 40 × e−5 = 40 × 0.006738 = 0.27 °C below the bath.
Sketch. An exponential rise from 0 towards the 40 °C line, with its initial slope A/τ = 20 °C/s meeting the final value at t = τ = 2 s, and the 63.2 % point marked at 2 s.

Assumptions. One time constant (a lumped bead, uniform temperature, τ = mc/(hA)); constant heat-transfer coefficient h; no self-heating from the excitation current; the bath stays at its new temperature. A sensor in a sheath has two thermal stores and lags more at the start than this model shows.

Why τ = mc/(hA). The heat entering the bead is hA(Tbath − T) and it raises the bead’s temperature: mc dT/dt = hA(Tbath − T). Dividing by hA gives (mc/hA) dT/dt + T = Tbath, the first-order equation with τ = mc/(hA). A bead twice the diameter has eight times the mass but only four times the area, so τ doubles; a stirred bath (larger h) shortens τ.
Check. The error halves every τ ln 2 = 1.39 s: 40 → 14.72 at 2 s, and 14.72 × e−4 = 0.27 at 10 s, consistent with the table.

bank.q: A second-order accelerometer has natural frequency 100 rad/s and damping ratio 0.2. Calculate the percentage overshoot and peak time for a step input, and comment on its usable frequency range.
outline: Percentage overshoot = 100 × e<sup>−πζ / √(1 − ζ²)</sup>.
For ζ = 0.2, overshoot ≈ 52.7%.
Peak time = π / (ωₙ√(1 − ζ²)) ≈ 0.032 s.
Low damping causes severe ringing near resonance.
For flat response, use ω well below ωₙ and prefer ζ near 0.6 to 0.8.
Sketch the step response.
answer: Data. ωn = 100 rad/s (fn = 100/2π = 15.9 Hz), ζ = 0.2, so the accelerometer is underdamped.
Damped frequency. ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²) = 100 × √0.96 = 97.98 rad/s.
Peak time. tp = π/ωd = π/97.98 = 0.0321 s = 32.1 ms.
Settling time (2 % band): ts ≈ 4/(ζωn) = 4/(0.2 × 100) = 0.20 s. The output rings through about 0.20/(2π/97.98) = 3 cycles before settling.

answer.text: Frequency response, ratio 1/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) with r = ω/ωn:

answer: Usable range. For a 5 % flat response at ζ = 0.2 the ratio 1/√((1 − r²)² + (0.4r)²) must stay below 1.05: this holds up to r ≈ 0.23, that is about 23 rad/s (3.7 Hz), under a quarter of ωn. Near resonance the sensor more than doubles the input (2.55 at 96 rad/s), so vibration there is badly over-read.

Remedy. Raise the damping to 0.6–0.7 (oil or eddy-current damping): at ζ = 0.7 the ratio stays within 1 % up to r ≈ 0.4 and within 3 % up to r = 0.5, and the step overshoot drops to 4.6 %. Or choose a sensor with ωn at least five times the highest frequency of interest.

Why it matters for an accelerometer. An accelerometer is a seismic mass m on a spring k with damper c: ωn = √(k/m) and ζ = c/(2√(km)). Its output follows acceleration only below ωn; above it the mass stays still and the sensor reads displacement instead. So ωn = 100 rad/s limits this sensor to slow motions such as vehicle body roll, not machine vibration.
Sketch. A step response overshooting to 1.527 at 32 ms and ringing down inside the ±2 % band by about 0.2 s.
Check. Overshoot and peak time use ωn in rad/s; using 100 Hz instead would give a wrong tp of 5.1 ms.

bank.q: Ten repeated readings of a voltage are 5.01, 4.99, 5.00, 5.02, 4.98, 5.00, 5.01, 4.99, 5.00 and 5.00 V. Calculate the mean, sample standard deviation, standard error and a 95% confidence interval.
outline: Mean = 5.000 V.
Compute deviations and sample standard deviation s.
Standard error = s / √n with n = 10.
95% confidence interval uses t ≈ 2.262 for 9 degrees of freedom.
Report result as mean ± expanded uncertainty with units.
Separate random uncertainty from any systematic calibration bias.
answer: Sample standard deviation. s² = Σd²/(n − 1) = 1200/9 = 133.3 mV²; s = √133.3 = 11.55 mV. The sum of deviations is zero, which checks the mean.
Standard error of the mean. sx̄ = s/√n = 11.55/√10 = 11.55/3.162 = 3.65 mV.

95 % confidence interval. With n − 1 = 9 degrees of freedom the Student t factor is 2.262. Half-width = 2.262 × 3.65 = 8.26 mV. Result: 5.000 V ± 8.3 mV (95 %, t = 2.262, n = 10), that is 4.992 V to 5.008 V.

Resolution term. The readings are given to 0.01 V, a rectangular uncertainty of ±5 mV, standard value 5/√3 = 2.89 mV. Combined with the scatter: √(3.65² + 2.89²) = 4.65 mV; with k = 2, ±9.3 mV. The resolution is not negligible here because the scatter is only about one display step.

Systematic part. This interval covers random scatter (and resolution) only. A calibration bias of the voltmeter, say ±5 mV from its certificate, is a separate Type B term and must be combined before the result is quoted as an accuracy.

Comparison with the worked example in the chapter. That set (5.01, 4.98, 5.02, 4.99, 5.00, 5.03, 4.97, 5.01, 4.99, 5.00 V) has the same mean but s = 18.26 mV, because two readings sit 30 mV out. This set is tighter, s = 11.55 mV, so its interval is narrower: ±8.3 mV against ±13.1 mV (2.262 × 5.77). The mean is the same; the confidence in it is not.
Check. Quoting s (11.6 mV) instead of s/√n (3.65 mV), or dividing by n instead of n − 1 (s = 10.95 mV), are the two usual slips; the factor 2.262 instead of 1.96 is what n = 10 costs.

bank.q: A neonatal weighing scale must measure from 0.1 kg to 20 kg with a resolution of 5 g. Choose a sensing principle, justify active or passive operation, and evaluate the static characteristics needed.
outline: Load cell with four strain gauges in a full Wheatstone bridge: passive
Justify against piezoelectric (no static reading)
Divisions needed and the signal per division
Non-linearity, hysteresis, creep and temperature drift within one division
Calibration with standard masses and traceability
Excitation, amplifier, ADC, filtering and hygiene
answer: Principle. A strain-gauge load cell: four foil gauges on a machined aluminium or steel element, wired as a full Wheatstone bridge, carry the weighing platform. The gauges change resistance by ΔR/R = GF·ε (GF ≈ 2) with the elastic strain of the element.

Active or passive. The bridge is passive: it needs an excitation voltage, and the output is proportional to it (rated output in mV/V). A piezoelectric (active) sensor is ruled out because a weight is a static force and the piezoelectric charge leaks away; it cannot hold a reading for the seconds a weighing takes. Passive operation also allows ratiometric measurement: the ADC reference is taken from the same excitation, so supply drift cancels.
Number of divisions. 20 kg/5 g = 4000 divisions. A 12-bit converter has 4096 codes, too few once noise and tare are allowed for; a 24-bit sigma-delta converter is used in practice.

Signal per division. Choose a 30 kg cell (50 % overload margin for a baby pushed down hard) with rated output 2 mV/V and 5 V excitation: 10 mV at 30 kg. At 20 kg the output is 10 × 20/30 = 6.67 mV, and one 5 g division is 6.67 mV × 5/20 000 = 1.67 µV. The amplifier’s input noise and drift must be well below this.

Static characteristics required. One division is 5/30 000 = 0.017 % of the rated capacity. So the combined non-linearity and hysteresis of the cell must stay near or below 0.017 % of rated output; creep (slow output change under constant load) must be smaller over the 10 to 30 s of a weighing; zero and span temperature drift must stay within one division over the room’s 15 to 35 °C, using the cell’s built-in compensation resistors.

head: Source
Requirement
rows: ≤ 5 g, or auto-zero at each tare

answer: Dynamic point. A baby moves, so the force fluctuates. A low-pass filter or averaging over 2 to 3 s steadies the reading, and the display waits until successive averages agree within one division.

Calibration. With traceable standard masses (for example 1, 5, 10 and 20 kg, each calibrated against secondary standards), up-scale and down-scale, at the clinic’s temperature; the certificate records non-linearity and hysteresis, and the scale is checked again after any shock.

Practical design. Shielded four- or six-wire cable (sense lines remove the cable’s voltage drop), a sealed, cleanable platform, overload stops, battery operation for isolation from mains leakage, and a tare key for the blanket.

Evaluation. The strain-gauge load cell meets the 5 g resolution with margin in electronics but only just in mechanics: the cell’s combined error class and creep decide the result, so they, not the ADC bits, set the specification.

bank.q: A calibration report shows zero drift of 0.5% span, hysteresis of 1% span and a linearity error of 0.8% span over a 0–200 kPa range. Evaluate whether the sensor suits a process needing ±1.5 kPa accuracy.
outline: Convert each error to kPa: span = 200 kPa.
Zero drift = 1.0 kPa; hysteresis = 2.0 kPa; linearity = 1.6 kPa.
Hysteresis alone exceeds the ±1.5 kPa limit.
Combine errors in the worst case and by root-sum-square.
Recommend recalibration, a better sensor or reduced range.
State that accuracy is not the same as resolution.
answer: Convert each error to kPa (span = 200 kPa): zero drift 0.5 % × 200 = 1.0 kPa; hysteresis 1 % × 200 = 2.0 kPa; non-linearity 0.8 % × 200 = 1.6 kPa.

Compare with the need. The process allows ±1.5 kPa. Hysteresis is a maximum up/down difference of 2.0 kPa: if the readings are referred to the mean curve, the error from it is ±1.0 kPa, and if to one curve, up to 2.0 kPa. Non-linearity alone, 1.6 kPa, already exceeds 1.5 kPa.
Verdict. Even the most generous combination, 2.14 kPa, is above 1.5 kPa, and the worst case is three times it. The sensor is not suitable as it is.

Options. (i) Correct the non-linearity: a calibration table or polynomial in the controller removes most of the 1.6 kPa, leaving √(1.0² + 1.0²) = 1.41 kPa RSS, just inside the limit. (ii) Remove zero drift by auto-zeroing at a known zero (vented line) before each batch: then hysteresis and the corrected non-linearity remain. (iii) Use a sensor with a 0–100 kPa range if the process stays below 100 kPa: the same percentages give half the kPa, 0.5, 1.0 and 0.8 kPa, RSS 1.37 kPa. (iv) Buy a better class sensor, for example ±0.25 %FS total.

Why hysteresis is treated as ±1.0 kPa. Hysteresis is the largest gap between the rising and falling curves. If the controller uses one mean calibration curve, a reading taken on either branch lies at most half the gap from it, ±1.0 kPa. If the controller uses the rising curve and the process is falling, the full 2.0 kPa appears. The worst-case column assumes the second case.
What not to argue. A fine resolution does not help; resolution is not accuracy. Repeating and averaging does not help either: hysteresis, non-linearity and drift are systematic and survive averaging.

A budget that would pass. Working back from ±1.5 kPa on a 200 kPa span: if the three terms are made equal and combined by RSS, each may be 1.5/√3 = 0.87 kPa, that is 0.43 %FS. So the purchase specification should read: zero drift, hysteresis (as ± from the mean curve) and non-linearity each ≤ 0.4 %FS, or a total accuracy ≤ ±0.75 %FS, with a recalibration interval short enough that drift stays inside its share.
Check. 0.5 + 1 + 0.8 = 2.3 % of 200 kPa = 4.6 kPa, the worst case above.

bank.q: A first-order sensor with time constant τ measures a ramp input of slope k. Derive the steady-state lag error and evaluate how τ affects the reading during a fast temperature rise.
outline: Model τ dy/dt + y = x(t), with x = kt.
Steady-state solution gives y = k(t − τ).
Lag error = kτ, proportional to slope and time constant.
Smaller τ gives smaller dynamic error.
For a step change, the error decays as e<sup>−t/τ</sup>.
Recommend sensor selection based on the fastest expected ramp.
answer: Model. A first-order sensor with unit sensitivity obeys τ dy/dt + y = x(t). The input is a ramp starting at t = 0: x = kt, with k in °C/s (or any unit per second), and y(0) = 0.

answer.text: Solve. Try a particular solution yp = at + b: τa + at + b = kt gives a = k and b = −kτ. The homogeneous solution is Ce−t/τ; y(0) = 0 gives C = kτ. So
answer.pre:
y(t) = k(t − τ) + kτ e<sup>−t/τ</sup>
     = kt − kτ(1 − e<sup>−t/τ</sup>)

answer: Error. e(t) = x − y = kτ(1 − e−t/τ). After a few time constants the exponential dies and the error settles to the steady-state lag error ess = kτ. The output is a ramp of the same slope, displaced by τ in time: the sensor shows now what the input was τ seconds ago.

answer.text: Numbers. A probe with τ = 2 s in a liquid heated at k = 2 °C/s:

answer: Effect of τ during a fast rise. The lag is proportional to both the rate and the time constant. Halving τ to 1 s halves the steady error to 2 °C; a slower 0.5 °C/s rise with τ = 2 s gives 1 °C. During the first τ or so the error builds up from zero, so a short heating pulse may end before the full lag appears.

Compare with a step. For a step A the error decays as Ae−t/τ and vanishes; for a ramp the error grows to kτ and stays as long as the ramp lasts. A controller that switches off a heater at a set temperature will overshoot by about kτ if it trusts the lagging reading.

Selection rule. For a fastest expected ramp kmax and an allowed dynamic error eallowed, choose τ ≤ eallowed/kmax. For 0.5 °C at 2 °C/s, τ ≤ 0.25 s: a fine bare-bead thermocouple, not a sheathed probe.

Frequency view. The same lag appears as a phase lag for a sinusoid: φ = tan⁻¹(ωτ). For slow inputs, ωτ is small and φ ≈ ωτ, a time delay of φ/ω = τ. So a first-order sensor behaves like a pure delay of τ at low frequency, which is exactly the ramp result.
Check. At t = 10 s the error is 4(1 − e−5) = 3.97 °C, within 1 % of kτ = 4 °C.

bank.q: Compare piezoresistive and capacitive MEMS pressure sensors for a tyre-pressure monitor. Consider sensitivity, temperature drift, power, size and signal conditioning.
outline: Piezoresistive: Wheatstone bridge, simple readout, moderate sensitivity, temperature drift.
Capacitive: high sensitivity, low power, needs capacitance-to-voltage circuitry.
Both can be micromachined and made small.
Tyre monitor needs wide temperature range and long battery life.
Evaluate drift, packaging and calibration cost.
Give a reasoned choice with trade-offs.
answer: Need. A tyre-pressure monitor sits inside the wheel: pressure around 200 to 250 kPa, temperature from below freezing to well above 100 °C after hard braking, strong shocks, and a sealed battery that must last for years. Power and drift decide the choice more than raw sensitivity.

Piezoresistive MEMS sensor. A thin silicon diaphragm with four diffused resistors in a Wheatstone bridge. Pressure bends the diaphragm; the resistors change by the piezoresistive effect, gauge factor 50 to 200, so the output is tens of millivolts at full scale and easy to read with a DC amplifier. Weak points: the bridge draws current whenever it is on, and silicon piezoresistance falls with temperature, so offset and span need temperature compensation.

Capacitive MEMS sensor. The diaphragm is one plate of a capacitor over a fixed electrode; pressure changes the gap: C = εA/d. A switched-capacitor readout charges a few picofarads, so the energy per reading is tiny and there is no standing current. Temperature effects are smaller because C depends on geometry, not on a temperature-sensitive resistivity. Weak points: C is non-linear in d (a 10 % gap reduction raises C by 11.1 %), the signal is a fraction of a picofarad, and stray capacitance must be guarded, so the readout chip is more complex.

answer.text: Power, worked. A 5 kΩ bridge at 3 V draws 3/5000 = 0.6 mA, that is 1.8 mW while on. Powered for 1 ms every 10 s, its average is 1.8 mW × 10⁻³ s/10 s = 0.18 µW. A capacitive readout with the same duty cycle typically averages well under that.

head: Point
Piezoresistive
Capacitive
rows: tens of mV full scale, linear
fraction of a pF, non-linear in d

answer: Calibration. Both are calibrated at several pressures and temperatures at the factory, and the coefficients are stored in the chip; the tyre monitor then corrects in firmware. Two-point zero and span checks are not enough when the temperature range is this wide.

Choice. For a battery-powered wheel unit the capacitive sensor wins on average power and temperature stability, and its non-linearity is removed by the stored calibration. A piezoresistive sensor is the better choice where power is not scarce and a simple, linear DC output is valued, for example a wired engine-oil pressure sender. Both must be packaged to survive the wheel’s shocks and the gel or filter that keeps dirt off the diaphragm.
Check. The duty-cycled bridge’s 0.18 µW is small, so a piezoresistive TPMS is possible; the decision is made on drift and on the total budget with the radio, not on the sensor alone.

glossary.def: A device that responds to a physical quantity and produces a measurable output.
A device that converts one form of energy into another, often a physical quantity into an electrical signal.
A device that converts an electrical signal into a physical action or quantity.
A self-generating sensor that produces an electrical output without an external excitation supply.
A sensor whose electrical property changes with the measurand and which needs an external supply.
The physical quantity that a sensor is intended to measure.
A transducer that converts an electrical signal back into a non-electrical physical quantity.
The process of comparing a sensor's output with a reference standard and recording the result.
A documented chain of comparisons linking a measurement to a recognised standard.
Checking that an instrument meets a stated specification or requirement.
A physical or software change made to bring an instrument's output closer to the true value.
The closeness of a measured value to the true value.
The closeness of repeated measurements to one another.
The smallest input change that produces a detectable output change.
The ratio of output change to input change, S = Δy/Δx.
The closeness of a sensor's calibration curve to a straight line.
The difference between output readings for the same input when approached from opposite directions.
A slow change in output with time or ambient conditions when the input is constant.
The difference between the upper and lower range limits; the output span is the matching difference of outputs.
The lower and upper limits of input over which a sensor is specified to operate.
The range of input change that produces no detectable change in output.
The time for a first-order sensor to reach 63.2% of its final response to a step input.
The ratio of actual damping to critical damping in a second-order system.
A repeatable error that shifts all readings by the same amount or in the same direction.
An unpredictable scatter in repeated readings that can be reduced by averaging.
A quantified range around a measured value within which the true value is expected to lie.
A national standard that realises an SI unit directly; used only to calibrate secondary standards.
A standard calibrated against the primary standard and held by a calibration laboratory.
A standard used every day to calibrate field instruments, checked against a secondary standard.
The guaranteed worst-case error of a reading or of a result computed from several readings.
